```{r}
library(pacman)
p_load(tidyverse, fpp3, BVAR)
```

## ARIMA vs. ETS

### 2.1 The Data

```{r}
liquor_raw <- read_csv(
  "data/MRTSSM4453USN.csv",
  na = ".",
  col_types = cols(
    observation_date = col_date(format = "%Y-%m-%d"),
    MRTSSM4453USN = col_double()
  )
)

liquor <- liquor_raw |>
  transmute(Month = yearmonth(observation_date), sales = MRTSSM4453USN) |>
  as_tsibble(index = Month) |>
  filter(Month <= yearmonth("2019 Dec"))

has_gaps(liquor)
```

```{r}
autoplot(liquor, sales) +
  labs(title = "Sales at Beer, Wine, and Liquor Stores",
       x = "Month",
       y = "Sales (millions of dollars)")

liquor |>
  gg_season(log(sales)) +
  labs(title = "Seasonal Plot of log(Sales) at Beer, Wine, and Liquor Stores",
       x = "Month",
       y = "log(Sales)")
```

Sales trend steadily upward over the whole sample, from about \$1.4 billion a month in early 1992 to over \$6 billion in December 2019. There are no big breaks in the trend. The seasonal pattern is very strong and repeats every year. December is by far the highest month and January and February are the lowest.

In the level plot, the seasonal swings clearly get bigger as the series grows. That means the seasonality is multiplicative. Taking logs turns that into an additive pattern.

### 2.2 Fit Both Models

```{r}
liquor_fit <- liquor |>
  model(arima = ARIMA(log(sales)),
        ets   = ETS(log(sales)))

liquor_fit |> select(arima) |> report()
liquor_fit |> select(ets) |> report()
```

fable chose an **ARIMA(1,0,2)(2,1,1)\[12\] with drift** and an **ETS(A,A,A)**.

The ARIMA has d = 0 and D = 1, so the series was seasonally differenced once and not regularly differenced.

For the ETS All three are additive. The errors are added to the forecast, the trend is a linear (not damped) trend, and the seasonal effects are added on.

```{r}
liquor_fit |> select(arima) |> gg_tsresiduals()

liquor_fit |>
  select(arima) |>
  augment() |>
  features(.innov, ljung_box, lag = 24, dof = 6)
```

I set dof = 6 because the ARIMA has p + q + P + Q = 1 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 6 estimated AR and MA coefficients.

The residuals do not look like white noise. The Ljung–Box statistic is about 120 with a p-value near zero, so I reject that the first 24 autocorrelations are all zero. The ACF has several significant spikes, the largest at lag 23, so there is structure the model hasn't captured.

### 2.3 The Horse Race

The TS-CV takes over 10 minutes, so I load the saved fits from my script.

```{r}
liquor_cv_fit <- readRDS("results/liquor_cv_fit.rds")

nrow(liquor_cv_fit)
```

The TS-CV uses **216 forecast origins**, with training samples ending from December 2001 through November 2019.

```{r}
liquor_cv_fc <- liquor_cv_fit |>
  forecast(h = 1)

range(liquor_cv_fc$Month)

liquor_cv_fc |>
  accuracy(liquor, measures = list(RMSE = RMSE, MAE = MAE)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

The first forecast is for **January 2002** and the last is for **December 2019**. ARIMA is the most accurate (RMSE about 81, MAE about 66), ETS is second, and the seasonal random walk is worst. RMSE and MAE agree on the ranking.

### 2.4 Are the Differences Significant?

```{r}
liquor_errs <- liquor_cv_fc |>
  as_tibble() |>
  left_join(as_tibble(liquor) |> select(Month, actual = sales),
            by = "Month") |>
  mutate(e = actual - .mean) |>
  select(Month, .model, e) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = .model, values_from = e)

# ARIMA vs. ETS
dm_ets <- forecast::dm.test(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$ets, h = 1, power = 2)

# ARIMA vs. seasonal random walk
dm_snaive <- forecast::dm.test(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$snaive, h = 1, power = 2)

tibble(Comparison = c("ARIMA vs. ETS", "ARIMA vs. SNAIVE"),
       `DM statistic` = c(dm_ets$statistic, dm_snaive$statistic),
       `p-value` = c(dm_ets$p.value, dm_snaive$p.value)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 4)
```

Both DM statistics are negative, so ARIMA has smaller squared errors in each comparison. ARIMA significantly beats ETS (DM = −2.91, p = 0.004) and the seasonal random walk (DM = −10.76, p roughly 0). I would use ARIMA: it wins on both metrics and the differences are significant.

## Forecast Combination

```{r}
liquor_combo_fc <- liquor_cv_fit |>
  mutate(combo = (arima + ets) / 2) |>
  forecast(h = 1)

liquor_combo_fc |>
  accuracy(liquor, measures = list(RMSE = RMSE, MAE = MAE)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

The combination falls between its two parts. It beats ETS but is worse than ARIMA on both RMSE (85.2) and MAE (66.8).

```{r}
cor(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$ets)
```

The ARIMA and ETS errors have a correlation of 0.88, so the models mostly miss in the same months and averaging cancels little error. Combining helps most when models are similarly accurate and their errors are less correlated, which isn't the case here.

## VAR vs. BVAR

### 4.1 The Data

```{r}
qd_raw <- read_csv("data/fredqd_2026-09.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  slice(-(1:2))

growth <- function(x) 100 * difference(log(x))

qd <- qd_raw |>
  mutate(date = as.Date(sasdate, "%m/%d/%Y")) |>
  transmute(date,
            gdp    = growth(GDPC1),         # real GDP
            cons   = growth(PCECC96),       # real consumption
            inv    = growth(GPDIC1),        # real investment
            emp    = growth(PAYEMS),        # payroll employment
            infl   = growth(GDPCTPI),       # GDP price index
            unrate = difference(UNRATE),    # unemployment rate
            ffr    = difference(FEDFUNDS),  # federal funds rate
            gs10   = difference(GS10)) |>   # 10-year Treasury yield
  filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))

y <- qd |> select(-date) |> as.matrix()

nrow(y)
head(y)

N <- nrow(y)
origins <- 120:(N - 1)
actual <- y[121:N, ]
```

There are **120 forecasts for each variable**, from **1990 Q1** to **2019 Q4**.

### 4.2 OLS VARs

```{r}
var_ols_fc <- function(z, p) {
  e <- embed(z, p + 1)            # columns: y_t, then its lags 1 to p
  M <- ncol(z)                    # number of variables
  B <- coef(lm(e[, 1:M] ~ e[, -(1:M)]))
  x <- c(1, t(z[nrow(z):(nrow(z) - p + 1), ]))   # constant, latest p lags
  x %*% B
}

fc_var1 <- NULL
fc_var4 <- NULL
for (T in origins) {
  fc_var1 <- rbind(fc_var1, var_ols_fc(y[1:T, ], 1))
  fc_var4 <- rbind(fc_var4, var_ols_fc(y[1:T, ], 4))
}

rmse_by_var <- function(f) sqrt(colMeans((actual - f)^2))

rmse_by_var(fc_var1)
rmse_by_var(fc_var4)
```

The VAR(1) forecasts better for 7 of 8 variables. The exception is inflation, where the VAR(4) wins by 0.001.

The VAR(4) always fits the training data at least as well, but it estimates 264 coefficients versus 72 for the VAR(1), with only 120 quarters in the first training sample.

### 4.3 A BVAR

The BVAR runs are in my script, so I load the saved forecasts and results table.

```{r}
fc_bvar_03  <- readRDS("results/fc_bvar_03.rds")
fc_bvar_005 <- readRDS("results/fc_bvar_005.rds")
var_results <- readRDS("results/var_results.rds")

var_results |> knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

**BVAR(4), λ = 0.3 vs. VAR(4).** The BVAR wins for all 8 variables. The difference is the Minnesota prior.

**BVAR(4), λ = 0.3 vs. VAR(1).** They are close. The BVAR wins for investment, inflation and the 10-year yield, and the VAR(1) wins for the other five.

**λ = 0.05.** Tighter shrinkage makes most forecasts worse (inflation goes from 0.197 to 0.330), though it is the best model for the fed funds rate.

**Is the winner's RMSE a fair estimate of future accuracy?** No. I pick the winner using the same test sample, so part of its edge is luck and its RMSE is biased downward.

```{r}
# GDP growth (column 1)
e_var4 <- actual[, "gdp"] - fc_var4[, 1]
e_bvar <- actual[, "gdp"] - fc_bvar_03[, 1]
dm_gdp <- forecast::dm.test(e_var4, e_bvar, h = 1, power = 2)

# Inflation (column 5)
e_var4_infl <- actual[, "infl"] - fc_var4[, 5]
e_bvar_infl <- actual[, "infl"] - fc_bvar_03[, 5]
dm_infl <- forecast::dm.test(e_var4_infl, e_bvar_infl, h = 1, power = 2)

tibble(Variable = c("GDP growth", "Inflation"),
       `DM statistic` = c(dm_gdp$statistic, dm_infl$statistic),
       `p-value` = c(dm_gdp$p.value, dm_infl$p.value)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

For GDP growth, DM = 2.14 (p = 0.035), so the BVAR is significantly more accurate at the 5% level. For inflation, DM = 1.45 (p = 0.149), so the difference isn't significant even though the BVAR has the lower RMSE.

So the BVAR beats the VAR(4) consistently, but not every gap in the 4.3b table is significant.

## Factor Model

### 5.1 The Data

```{r}
md_raw <- read_csv("data/fredmd_2026-09.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
tcode <- unlist(md_raw[1, -1])
md <- md_raw[-1, ] |> mutate(date = as.Date(sasdate, "%m/%d/%Y"))

transform_series <- function(x, code) {
  d <- function(v) c(NA, diff(v))
  switch(as.character(code),
         "1" = x,                      # level
         "2" = d(x),                   # first difference
         "3" = d(d(x)),                # second difference
         "4" = log(x),                 # log
         "5" = 100 * d(log(x)),        # growth rate
         "6" = 100 * d(d(log(x))),     # change in the growth rate
         "7" = d(x / dplyr::lag(x) - 1))
}

fm <- map2_dfc(md[names(tcode)], tcode, transform_series) |>
  mutate(date = md$date, .before = 1) |>
  filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))

fm <- fm[, colSums(is.na(fm)) == 0]

dim(fm)

tcode[c("INDPRO", "PAYEMS", "CPIAUCSL", "FEDFUNDS")]
```

After the transformations, the data has 718 rows and 122 columns.

- **INDPRO (code 5):** monthly growth rate, 100 × the change in log.
- **PAYEMS (code 5):** monthly growth rate, same as INDPRO.
- **CPIAUCSL (code 6):** change in the monthly inflation rate.
- **FEDFUNDS (code 2):** first difference, the monthly change in percentage points.

### 5.2 Estimate the Factors

```{r}
Z <- fm |> select(-date) |> as.matrix()

pc <- prcomp(scale(Z))

summary(pc)$importance[, 1:5]
```

The first three factors explain about **29.5%** of the variation (15.0%, 7.4% and 7.1%).

```{r}
F1 <- pc$x[, 1] * sign(cor(pc$x[, 1], fm$INDPRO))

tibble(date = fm$date, F1 = F1) |>
  ggplot(aes(date, F1)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "First Factor from FRED-MD", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
sort(abs(cor(pc$x[, 1], Z))[1, ], decreasing = TRUE)[1:8]
sort(abs(cor(pc$x[, 2], Z))[1, ], decreasing = TRUE)[1:8]
```

The **first factor** is most correlated with employment, industrial production and capacity utilization (PAYEMS, IPMANSICS, USGOOD, INDPRO, MANEMP, IPFPNSS, CUMFNS, DMANEMP).

The **second factor** is most correlated with CPI and PCE price indexes (such as CPIAUCSL, PCEPI and CPITRNSL), so it is probably an inflation factor.

### 5.3 Replicate the Horse Race from Class

```{r}
ip <- fm$INDPRO
n <- nrow(Z)
init <- which(fm$date == as.Date("1989-12-01"))

e_ar <- NULL
e_fa <- NULL
for (T in init:(n - 1)) {
  F_T <- prcomp(scale(Z[1:T, ]))$x[, 1:3]         # factors using data through T
  d <- data.frame(y_next = ip[2:T], y = ip[1:(T - 1)], F_T[1:(T - 1), ])
  new <- data.frame(y = ip[T], t(F_T[T, ]))
  e_ar <- c(e_ar, ip[T + 1] - predict(lm(y_next ~ y, d), new))
  e_fa <- c(e_fa, ip[T + 1] - predict(lm(y_next ~ ., d), new))
}

c(RMSE_AR = sqrt(mean(e_ar^2)), RMSE_FA = sqrt(mean(e_fa^2)))
```

I get RMSEs of 0.617 for the AR(1) and 0.589 with the factors, matching class.

Estimating the factors on the full sample would use data from after each forecast origin, which a real forecaster wouldn't have.

### 5.4 A Direct Forecast of Inflation

```{r}
direct_race <- function(series, h = 12, r = 3) {
  lv <- md |>
    mutate(log_x = log(.data[[series]]),
           g = 100 * (log_x - lag(log_x))) |>
    filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))
  yh <- 100 * (lead(lv$log_x, h) - lv$log_x)   # growth over the next h months
  g  <- lv$g                                   # growth over the latest month

  e_ar <- NULL
  e_fa <- NULL
  for (T in init:(n - h)) {
    F_T <- prcomp(scale(Z[1:T, ]))$x[, 1:r, drop = FALSE]
    i <- 1:(T - h)   # only targets already observed at origin T
    d <- data.frame(yh = yh[i], g = g[i], F_T[i, , drop = FALSE])
    new <- data.frame(g = g[T], F_T[T, , drop = FALSE])
    e_ar <- c(e_ar, yh[T] - predict(lm(yh ~ g, d), new))
    e_fa <- c(e_fa, yh[T] - predict(lm(yh ~ ., d), new))
  }

  tibble(series, forecasts = length(e_ar),
         RMSE_AR = sqrt(mean(e_ar^2)), RMSE_FA = sqrt(mean(e_fa^2)),
         MAE_AR = mean(abs(e_ar)), MAE_FA = mean(abs(e_fa)),
         DM_pvalue = forecast::dm.test(e_ar, e_fa, h = h, power = 2,
                                       varestimator = "bartlett")$p.value)
}

direct_race("CPIAUCSL") |> knitr::kable(digits = 4)
```

Yes. The factors cut the RMSE from 2.11 to 1.89, about 10.4%, and the DM p-value is 0.0004, so the improvement is significant.

## Reflection

Simple models are hard to beat: the VAR(1) beat the VAR(4), and the combination couldn't beat ARIMA. Models with many freely estimated parameters end up fitting noise. Shrinkage, equal weights and factors all fix this the same way, by imposing structure instead of estimating every coefficient separately. Too much structure hurts too, as λ = 0.05 showed. I also learned to check DM tests before trusting a ranking, since many of the RMSE differences weren't significant.g
